newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Supplies, weak demand pressure Asian LSWR prices.
newsitem.headline: Supplies, weak demand pressure Asian LSWR prices.

text.p: Prices of Asian low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR), a fuel for power generation, are under pressure as Indonesia raises exports amid weak demand, industry sources said on Thursday.
Traders in Singapore said regional demand in October would total 2.56 million barrels but supplies from Indonesia, the region's main exporter of LSWR, were more than 4.2 million barrels.
They said even conservative estimates, should spot demand emerge, would indicate at least half a million barrels of surplus LSWR could remain unsold by the end of October.
Industry sources have estimated Japan and South Korea would each absorb 800,000 barrels of LSWR in October, India will take in 400,000 barrels and Italy, its usual term supply of 560,000 barrels.
A Japanese trader told Reuters that imports from Japan have remained depressed this month as domestic utility prices were under international spot market levels.
"It does not make economic sense to import until we adjust retail prices," he said.

Earlier this week, Indonesian state oil company Pertamina added 400,000 barrels to the already well-supplied market. Its initial allocation for October, made in late September, was 3.8 million barrels or 200,000 barrels more than its September allocation.
The additional allocation was a result of a surplus following a delay in starting up a 55,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) visbreaker at Pertamina's Cilacap refinery earlier in October.
LSWR is fed into a visbreaker to reduce its viscosity, or to lighten its waxy texture and to produce naphtha and middle distillates.
Sources said Pertamina may even have more LSWR for export in October as traditionally it has made an additional allocation of up to 400,000 barrels per month.
Traders said they believed current benchmark LSWR prices in the Singapore spot market at around $20.30-$20.40 per barrel were too high which was discouraging buying interest.
They said prices would have to fall by at least a dollar a barrel to attract buyers back to the market.
Another Japanese trader said South Korea was raising production of LSWR for the time being because import prices are so high.
Traders said there is also no buying interest from the U.S., an alternative outlet for Asian barrels for either burning in the winter season or processing into gasoline during the summer months.
They said the economics of trading Asia LSWR into the U.S. was difficult anyhow because of high benchmark prices in Singapore.
Traders said the poor demand for LSWR has already taken its toil on the premium for Indonesian LSWR.
The premium for LSWR over benchmark prices has fallen to around 30 cents from 50 cents in the past week, they said.
